paras: The lynching of Johnson and "Tex" took place at American Falls, Idaho Territory, on the night of Sunday, 8 October 1882, when townsmen hanged two men they suspected of murdering a Chinese man from the Oregon Short Line Railroad bridge over the Snake river. The hanging followed an order to leave town and a gunfight with the citizens and the night watchman. An Ogden account carried the story through Idaho, Utah, Nevada, California and Montana papers, and no report gives the race of either man.

According to the Ogden Pilot, the two men, known only as Johnson and "Tex," had been "loafing" around American Falls through the summer and had "incurred the enmity of the law-abiding citizens," some of whom resolved to run them out of town. A Chinese man was then found dead in his cabin, or, in another phrasing, killed while asleep in his tent, and his body was taken to Ogden. Suspicion fell on the two men, and an Ogden dispatch said he had been killed "for his money."

The citizens gave the pair until 8 o'clock on Sunday night to leave. In the Pilot's account the men answered that "there were not men enough at American Falls to make them leave" and fired into the crowd, which armed itself and returned fire, after which the two fled across the Snake river threatening to come back and "clean out the town." On their return they met the night watchman, who told them they would be hanged; they fired three shots at him and missed, and he wounded Johnson three times with his revolver.

When Tex rushed the watchman, who had run out of ammunition, the watchman threw him down, and at that point the citizens arrived and seized both men. The shorter Ogden dispatch said the men were "overpowered, taken to" the railroad bridge, where the citizens put ropes around their necks and hanged them. The bodies were cut down three hours later and buried by the citizens.

No report of an inquest, arrests or any official inquiry appears in the coverage. The White Pine News of Nevada suggested that "Tex" was probably a man who had spent the previous winter and spring at Cherry Creek, where he was thought "a harmless, inoffensive sort of fellow."

The story reached the press in two forms: a short Ogden dispatch of 10 October, printed the next day in Sacramento and Salt Lake City, and a fuller Ogden Pilot account reprinted by the Wood River Times, the Ketchum Keystone and the White Pine News, among others. Both versions called the men "desperadoes" and their killers "the citizens," and the Sacramento Daily Record-Union headed its item "Two Desperadoes Disposed Of."

Some editors treated the affair with irony: a Salt Lake paper ran the dispatch under "Justice to Heathens," and the White Pine News called it a "little frolic." Farther away the story was garbled, as when the Maysville Evening Bulletin placed it at Ogden and said the men were caught murdering a watchman, and the Batesville Guard had them hanged from a tree, adding, "They had done nothing but murder a Chinaman." None of the reports describes either victim as Black.

The Pilot account, dated by the Ketchum Keystone to Sunday the 8th, has the men ordered out by 8 o'clock that night, while the Ogden dispatch has the murder on Sunday night and the order to leave on Monday, and one copy of it says Saturday night.

bases: Citizens of American Falls seized two men suspected of murdering a Chinese man and hanged them from a railroad bridge without any legal process (A1, A6, A10).

The 'citizens' who had resolved to run the two out of town seized them and hanged them from the Oregon Short Line bridge, on suspicion of murdering a Chinese man (A1, A6, A10). The race of the two men is never given, so the episode's place in a study of anti-Black violence is doubtful.
Every detailed report traces to the Ogden Pilot or an Ogden dispatch (A1, A2, A6, A9, A10); the two versions agree on the core event but no independent local account appears.
